title: *Extended Topic* Microscopy Enhanced by the Wave Characteristics of Light
short: Microscopy and the waves of light
lead: The wave nature of light limits the detail a microscope can show, since you cannot see details much smaller than a wavelength. Microscopes also turn the same wave characteristics to their advantage. Interference, phase and polarization give contrast to nearly transparent objects, and a confocal pinhole images one plane of a thick specimen at a time.
objectives: Discuss the different types of microscopes.
summary_html: • To improve microscope images, various techniques utilizing the wave characteristics of light have been developed. Many of these enhance contrast with interference effects.

figures.original_caption: Light rays passing through a sample under a microscope will emerge with different phases depending on their paths. The object shown has a greater index of refraction than the background, and so the wavelength decreases as the ray passes through it. Superimposing these rays produces interference that varies with path, enhancing contrast between the object and background.

exercises.prompt: Explain how microscopes can use wave optics to improve contrast and why this is important.

answer.solution: Many microscopic objects absorb very little light, so they differ little in intensity from the background and are hard to see. Light passing through such an object still travels through a different index of refraction, so it holds a different number of wavelengths and emerges out of phase with light from the background. An interference or phase-contrast microscope superimposes the two, and the phase difference turns into a difference in brightness through constructive and destructive interference. A polarization microscope does the same with polarizing filters. The contrast makes nearly transparent objects, such as living cells, visible without stains.

exercises.prompt: A bright white light under water is collimated and directed upon a prism. What range of colors does one see emerging?

answer.solution: One still sees the full range of colors, from red to violet, since the colors are set by the frequencies of the light and these do not change in water. The prism disperses the light because its index of refraction depends on the wavelength, but the glass and the water are closer in index than the glass and air, so each color bends less at the surfaces and the spectrum is spread over a smaller angle than it would be in air.
